title: From Pani Puri to Prix Fixe: Sujan Sarkar's Michelin Empire Lands in New York and Phoenix
excerpt: The first Bengali chef to earn a Michelin star in America opens two restaurants in five weeks, stretching Indian fine dining from Hudson Yards to the Arizona desert.
body:
In the space of five weeks, chef Sujan Sarkar has opened two Indian restaurants in two cities he had never operated in before — and both are already turning heads. Indienne, his Michelin-starred fine-dining flagship, debuted at Hudson Yards in Manhattan on May 28. Nadu, his regional Indian concept, opened at Desert Ridge Marketplace in Phoenix on June 26. For the Indian diaspora watching from the sidelines, Sarkar's rapid expansion tells a bigger story: Indian cuisine is no longer knocking on the door of American fine dining. It is kicking it open.

The Kolkata-born chef has spent over two decades building toward this moment. After cutting his teeth in Michelin-starred kitchens across London, he launched ROOH in San Francisco in 2017 — a progressive Indian restaurant that earned a three-star review from the *San Francisco Chronicle* and the Golden Gate Restaurant Association's Best New Restaurant award in its debut year. ROOH's success led to outposts in Chicago, New Delhi, and Palo Alto, and established Sarkar as a chef capable of translating Indian cuisine for a global audience without dulling its edges.

## The Michelin Star That Changed Everything

In 2022, Sarkar opened Indienne in Chicago's River North neighbourhood, and within a year it became the city's first — and still only — Michelin-starred Indian restaurant. The honour made Sarkar the first Bengali chef in the United States to earn a Michelin star, and it placed Indienne alongside Semma and Bungalow in an elite cohort of just four Michelin-starred Indian restaurants in the country.

The New York outpost is intimate — just 34 seats inside the luxury residential tower Henry Hall — and unapologetically ambitious. Three nine-course tasting menus (non-vegetarian at $195, vegetarian and vegan at $175 each) begin with playful, chaat-inspired courses before moving into seasonal compositions layered with spice and technique. The opener is a signature oyster *pani puri* that has already become one of the most photographed dishes on Manhattan restaurant feeds. A Wine Spectator Award of Excellence-winning beverage programme completes the picture.

Sarkar isn't stopping there. Two more concepts — Elder, a British-Indian chophouse, and Apas, a cocktail bar — are expected to open inside Henry Hall later this summer.

## Nadu Brings the Village Kitchen to Phoenix

While Indienne speaks the language of fine dining, Nadu speaks the language of home. The name means "homeland" in Tamil, and the concept celebrates dishes from more than ten regions of India — the kind of cooking that rarely appears on American menus. Dahi Bhalla chaat, Benne Masala Dosa, and duck kebabs sit alongside a rotating selection of preparations that change with the seasons and the produce available from Arizona farms.

Nadu's Chicago flagship had already earned a Bib Gourmand designation and an Eater National Best New Restaurant nod within its first year. Phoenix is only the second city to get one. The 120-seat space features bold oil paintings by Chicago artist Abhay Sehgal, whose commissioned piece "The Chicago Durbar" has become an attraction in its own right — Indian deities mingling with basketball players in front of the Chicago Theatre, and a king presenting a Dior Nike sneaker as a gift.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs watching Sarkar's rise, the significance goes beyond restaurant openings. A decade ago, the highest-profile Indian restaurants in America were still largely clustered in New York and the Bay Area. Sarkar's expansion into Phoenix — alongside his partnership with Zest Hospitality Group, the team behind Chandler's acclaimed Feringhee — signals that Indian fine dining is now viable in mid-market American cities, not just coastal food capitals.

"I want to be a true representation of Indian food in America, which can be on par with the top restaurants in the city and the country — and in the world," Sarkar has said.

With a James Beard nomination for Best Chef: Great Lakes in both 2024 and 2025, and now a Michelin-starred tasting room in Manhattan, the first Bengali chef to earn a star in America is building something larger than a restaurant group. He is building a case that Indian cuisine deserves to be discussed in the same breath as French, Japanese, and Scandinavian cooking — not as an emerging curiosity, but as an established pillar of global gastronomy.
